about.title: About the product
about.text: A schedule service for universities and apps for students.

window.lead: A service where a university keeps its schedule, and apps where students and teachers see it. This is the product’s new version: all three client apps have been rewritten from scratch since 2 June 2026.

what.title: What it is
what.p1: At a university, the academic office makes the schedule. In Pora na Paru it lives in one place, and changes reach the iOS and Android apps, the widgets and the website at once. Groups, teachers and rooms each have a schedule of their own.

now.title: What already works
now.p1: The browser schedule has been open since 16 October 2026: the week of any group, teacher or room via a link, with nothing to install. The iOS and Android apps are in alpha testing: the iOS store build has been with testers in TestFlight since 27 September, and the Android build in a closed test on Google Play since 30 September. Anyone can try them: the links are in those lessons’ windows. The website poranaparu.com has been live since 30 September.
now.p2: The editor for universities is being designed: in it, schedules will be built and published to every app with one button.

role.title: My role
role.p1: I am a co-founder and the CEO. I design the interfaces in Figma and write all three clients myself: iOS in SwiftUI, Android in Jetpack Compose, the web in Next.js. The backend and the server side are my co-founder’s.

how.title: How the work is done
how.p1: Each client is a separate repository with its own knowledge base: feature specs, a decision log and automated checks. Decisions go into the log, so you can see not only how something was built but why.

origin.title: The start: VCourse
origin.text: The first version. Launched on 1 September 2025; 632 downloads in three days.

window.lead: The product’s first version. It tested the idea on real users.

why.title: Where the idea came from
why.p1: Checking my own class schedule was a pain. Some universities had their own apps for that, and from 2023 a classmate and I talked about building one for ours, but kept putting it off: the idea seemed too big.

build.title: How we made it
build.p1: In our third year, in September 2024, we were given a semester to build a product on an idea of our own. I took product design and the frontend, my classmate the backend and DevOps. I had no experience in mobile development: the first semester went on Swift, SwiftUI, Xcode and the iOS guidelines.
build.p2: The next semester and the summer went into polishing. The app was rewritten from scratch several times.

launch.title: The launch
launch.p1: On 1 September 2025 a post came out in the university’s Telegram channel, and strangers began to download the app. In the first three days: 632 downloads, 411 of them on 2 September.
launch.p2: Within a semester of the launch, the Android app and the website came out and five more institutions joined. Then came the question of what would sustain the product: that is “The fork”, on Tuesday.

fork.title: The fork
fork.text: Ads in the app or a service for universities. We chose the service.

window.lead: After VCourse launched, we had to decide what the product would run on: ads in the student app or a service for universities. We chose the service.

question.title: The question
question.p1: In the semester after the launch, the Android app and the website came out and five more institutions joined. The app was free and had no ads, and we could not develop it seriously while earning nothing from it.

ceiling.title: The app’s ceiling
ceiling.p1: VCourse pulled schedules from universities’ websites. Any redesign of such a site broke the schedule in the app, and the university itself got nothing from the app.
ceiling.p2: The only way to earn from it was ads. We did not want to put them in.

heard.title: What we heard
heard.p1: Students learn about changes from chats, from their class reps or only once they are in the room: the official schedule does not show last-minute changes.
heard.p2: In the academic office, the standard system cannot handle a one-off teacher substitution: the lesson is cancelled and the dean’s office phones the students. The team ran the interviews with students and academic offices.

choice.title: What we chose
choice.p1: A service in which the academic office makes the schedule itself and publishes it to every app at once. The university becomes the source of the data, and the students’ apps become part of the service.
choice.p2: VCourse has not been updated since February 2026. In April we pitched to investors at the Tramplin tech park with the service for universities, and on 2 June we started the new version, Pora na Paru.

ios.title: The iOS app
ios.text: SwiftUI, Live Activity and widgets. The build is in TestFlight.

window.lead: A native app in SwiftUI: the schedule, notes, widgets, Live Activity and Siri shortcuts. Since 27 September 2026 its store build has been with testers in TestFlight.

try.title: Try it
try.p1: The alpha is open to anyone with the link: TestFlight, Apple’s beta testing app, installs and updates it. You need an iPhone with iOS 17 or later.

what.title: What it does
what.p1: The week of a group, a teacher or a room, subgroups, search across six directories and in Spotlight. A lesson can carry a note with photos and a reminder.
what.p2: The schedule is kept on the phone and opens offline: the Storage screen shows what is saved and how much room it takes.

outside.title: Outside the app
outside.p1: A Live Activity keeps the current lesson on the lock screen and in the Dynamic Island, and moves on by itself from lesson to break to the end of the day. The server does not send updates yet, so the card carries its next phase in advance and switches to it on the schedule it already knows.
outside.p2: There are nine widgets: six on the lock screen and three on the home screen — notes you can tick off right in the widget, favourites and a lesson calendar. Plus eight Siri shortcuts and quick actions on the app icon.

reminders.title: Reminders
reminders.p1: Notifications are set by rules rather than a bell on each lesson: reminders for notes, morning and evening summaries of the day, and important lessons — office hours, tests and exams. The system allows an app 64 scheduled notifications; the app keeps its queue at 60.

how.title: How it is built
how.p1: Swift 6 and SwiftUI, iOS 17 and later, Liquid Glass on iOS 26. Six modules on Tuist, storage on SwiftData, and one external dependency: a snapshot testing library.
how.p2: The store build and the internal one, with made-up data, are two different targets: the test data cannot reach the store even by mistake.

android.title: The Android app
android.text: Compose and Material 3 Expressive, the current lesson in a widget.

window.lead: A native app in Jetpack Compose with Material 3 Expressive. The alpha reaches testers through closed testing on Google Play.

try.title: Try it
try.p1: The alpha installs from Google Play and updates like any other app. The closed test is open to anyone who joins the testers’ group. You need a phone with Android 10 or later and Google Play.

what.title: What it does
what.p1: The same as on iOS, but by Android’s rules: the week of a group, a teacher or a room, subgroups, search across the directories, notes with photos and notifications. Buildings have maps.
what.p2: The schedule is kept on the phone and opens offline.

widgets.title: Widgets
widgets.p1: Four Glance widgets: favourites, a lesson calendar, notes you can tick off without opening the app, and a first version of a current-lesson widget. Android has no Live Activity, so a widget shows the current lesson: a system timer counts the minutes, and the progress bar moves once a minute.

colour.title: Colour
colour.p1: Seventeen accents to choose from. From each one Material 3 builds a light and a dark scheme; all 34 schemes are exported from the generator in advance rather than computed on the phone.

how.title: How it is built
how.p1: Kotlin, Compose, Android 10 and later. Eleven Gradle modules, Hilt, Room and Navigation 3. In tests a network request interceptor stands in for the server, and the store build is checked to make sure no test data got into it.
how.p2: The privacy check found seven permissions in the build instead of two: libraries had added five of them.

web.title: The schedule in a browser
web.text: The whole week via a link, with nothing to install. Live since 16 October 2026.

window.lead: The week of any group, teacher or room via a link, with nothing to install. Live since 16 October 2026.

what.title: What it does
what.p1: The week grid follows the university’s bell times: today is highlighted, the current lesson has a ring and the time left, and a line marks the current time. The page opens already scrolled to the nearest lesson, and you can page through weeks for years forward and back.
what.p2: ⌘K search covers groups, teachers, rooms, faculties, departments and buildings. Each lesson has its own window, each room its building’s map, and subgroups switch with tabs.

time.title: The university’s time
time.p1: “Now”, “today” and the time left are counted in the university’s time zone: a student looking at the schedule from another city sees the same as someone in the room.

how.title: How it is built
how.p1: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4 and shadcn/ui on Radix. The pages are rendered on the server and refreshed every five minutes, and only the server talks to the API.
how.p2: 17 automated checks: accessibility to WCAG 2.2 AA in both themes, addresses, SEO and the JavaScript budget. The schedule screen has a 250 KB gzip budget; the week grid weighed 196.6 KB as of 18 October 2026.

phone.title: On a phone
phone.p1: For now it is a plain list of lessons by day. A full phone layout is still to come, and the pages stay closed to search engines until the schedule takes its final shape.

system.title: The design system
system.text: One set of Figma tokens and the same lesson type colours on every platform.

window.lead: One palette and one set of lesson type colours on iOS, Android and the web. Each platform gets there its own way.

one.title: A lesson’s type is a colour
one.p1: A lecture, a practical or an exam is recognisable by its colour on any screen: in a card, a widget or a lesson’s window. In the light theme it is shade 500 of the Tailwind palette; in the dark theme, 300.

figma.title: From Figma to code
figma.p1: Figma variables are exported as a snapshot in the W3C Design Tokens format: 527 tokens in 11 files. A script builds the web CSS from the snapshot, with light and dark values in pairs.
figma.p2: The Tokens check lets no commit through if the CSS has drifted from the snapshot: colours are changed in Figma, not in code.

platforms.title: Three platforms
platforms.p1: On iOS the same values are written in Swift. Android takes the shade as a seed: the Material 3 generator builds the roles for the light and the dark theme from it, and a check forbids hard-coded colours and sizes outside the design system module.
platforms.p2: The three clients share the palette and the mapping of lesson type to shade. Everything else each platform does by its own rules: HIG on iOS, Material 3 Expressive on Android.

here.title: On this page
here.p1: The week and the lesson windows here are built on the same values: the brand’s blue, zinc greys, the type colours and the Geist typeface. Sizes are scaled up 1.25 times.

editor.title: The editor
editor.text: Catches conflicts before publishing. Still being designed.

window.lead: A workspace where the academic office will make the schedule and publish it to every app at once. It is being designed; there is no code yet.

what.title: What it will be
what.p1: The release features were set out on 29 September 2026: the schedule editor, directories, publishing to every app, change notifications, import and integrations, and roles.
what.p2: In the editor, lessons are dragged and dropped, weeks are built from templates, and subgroups and substitutions are part of the schedule. A room or a teacher booked for two lessons at once is highlighted before publishing.

pain.title: Where it starts
pain.p1: The first scenario: someone in the academic office replaces a teacher who is ill. Today the standard system cannot handle such a substitution, and the design starts there.

before.title: What VCourse taught
before.p1: I designed the first editor of this kind for VCourse. A conflict there was only a clash of resources: one teacher, room or group in two places at once. Subgroups meeting in parallel did not count as a conflict.
before.p2: Any edit could be undone, and publishing went in two steps: a summary of all the changes, a check on the server, and only then a write in a single transaction. A contradictory schedule could not be published. My co-founder built the server check.

now.title: Now
now.p1: The workspace will come after account sign-in. Screens for the scenarios are being drawn in Figma.

code.title: The new version’s code
code.p1: 2,642 commits in three clients over five months. iOS came first, Android started on 10 August and the web on 29 September, and the months show the work moving from one client to the next.

sources.p2: Usage numbers are published with my co-founder’s consent. They are recounted before each publication.

stores.title: Stores
stores.p1: Every feature of the iOS app is done. Next come checks on devices with iOS 17, 18 and 26, and the App Store release.
stores.p2: The Android app is in alpha testing through a closed test on Google Play. Live Activities on the iPhone will start updating from the server once the server can send them.

cabinet.title: The university’s workspace
cabinet.p1: Then the workspace, where the academic office makes the schedule and publishes it to every app with one button, and conflicts show before publishing. That is the subject of “The editor”, on Thursday.
